idiom_name: ordered predicate table (rules as data) selecting a named output channel, with an explicit fallback route
implementation_notes:
Language-neutral form: decode enough of the message to reach the routing fields, then evaluate an ordered list of rules - each a predicate over the decoded content plus the destination it selects - and forward the message unchanged to the first destination whose rule matches. Keep the rules as data (a table, a configuration document, a DSL route) rather than as a growing if/else chain, so the routing matrix can be reviewed and tested, and always include a fallback destination (Invalid Message Channel, Dead Letter Channel or an explicitly named default) because an unmatched message has nowhere to go. Keep the router stateless and free of payload mutation: selecting a destination is the whole responsibility, and enrichment or reshaping belongs at the destination handler.

Service-mesh realization: In Istio service mesh, the VirtualService defines HTTP match rules that constitute a Content-Based Router at the mesh layer. Rules are evaluated top-to-bottom (first match wins). Custom headers (e.g., x-tenant-id), query parameters, or URI prefixes can all serve as the routing discriminator. Gateways and DestinationRules define the actual network endpoints and subsets (e.g., v1, v2). This pattern is particularly valuable for canary deployments, A/B testing, and multi-tenant routing without application-level code changes. Workloads are unaware of the routing decisions.
code_sketch:
route(msg):
    decoded = decode_envelope(msg)                 # only what the rules need
    for rule in RULES:                             # ordered: first match wins
        if rule.matches(decoded):
            return send(rule.destination, msg)     # message forwarded unchanged
    return send(FALLBACK_CHANNEL, msg)             # never drop silently
pitfalls: Routing on a field that was never validated: a missing or mistyped discriminator falls through every rule and lands in the fallback, so fallback volume is the metric that reveals schema drift.
Letting the router mutate, enrich or reformat the payload: it then needs the union of every destination's needs and stops being replaceable.
Rules as an if/else chain inside the router: the routing matrix cannot be tested, reviewed or changed without editing code that all traffic crosses.
Inline string destinations inside conditions: channel names should be constants to prevent typos and enable refactoring.

Synchronous external lookups inside routing predicates: causes temporal coupling (latency spikes affect every message) and risks partial failure if the lookup service is unavailable - enrich data before routing instead.
Deeply nested rule conditions (>3 levels): becomes unreadable and unmaintainable; prefer a flat chain of modular predicates or extract rules into a separate configuration artifact.

In broker-based routing (Azure Service Bus, Amazon SQS): relying on body fields when the broker rule language only supports properties/headers; always promote discriminator fields to message properties at publish time.

Forgetting that broker-level filters (JMS selectors, Azure Service Bus filters, AMQP header exchanges) run inside the broker, so adding many rules increases broker CPU load; in-process routing may be preferable for complex rule sets.

A CBR that forks to N destinations cannot use parent-child spans: a span can only have a single parent, so each consumer must LINK to the message creation context rather than being its child, and the router must re-emit producer/consumer spans to keep the trace intact.

A router that republishes without extracting or propagating the original trace context breaks the trace at exactly the hop where observability matters most; propagate the original traceparent through application-properties or message-annotations and never clobber the producer's context.

OTel messaging semantic conventions are still in Development status; dashboards and alerts keyed on router span or attribute names need OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN to avoid dashboard breakage when names change.

Routing metrics can explode cardinality under high fan-out: OTel's SDK default cardinality limit is 2000 points per instrument per collection cycle; label explosion from destination x rule x tenant x message-type collapses into the overflow bucket precisely under load — keep per-message routing detail on spans.

Auto-registering schemas at runtime lets a producer redefine the routing surface in production; pre-register in CI/CD with auto.register.schemas=false so the schema evolution gate stays outside the hot path.

Record-based subject name strategies (RecordNameStrategy, TopicRecordNameStrategy) let the set of types in a topic grow unbounded, breaking ksqlDB, Flink and any router that needs to enumerate the routing domain — prefer topic-based naming with union types.

Backward-compatible schema evolution guarantees parsers survive but does not guarantee a discriminator value keeps meaning the same destination; every union-member addition is a routing-table change that must ship alongside the schema change.

Semantic or learned routing turns routing errors into quality regressions: there is no delivery-error signal that says a request went to the wrong model, so the routing policy needs offline evaluation, shadow traffic and a documented rollback path.

Adaptive latency-based routing can silently degrade to weighted random selection if the latency cache suffers from lost-update races (observed 80/20 distribution with real provider latencies differing by 10x); monitor achieved-vs-intended distribution, not only configured rules.

PHI or PII in routing keys, queue names, headers, filter policies or mesh route names is a disclosure; by HIPAA §164.312 and AWS HIPAA eligibility rules, only BAA-covered services may carry ePHI and the routing decision itself must not leak the identifier.

FHIR subscriptions remain active after the authorization that created them expires; a routing decision based on subscription criteria outlives the access grant and may continue routing to a destination no longer authorized for the data.
A healthcare CBR needs a suppression path, not just destinations: routing the existence of a record is itself a disclosure when consent has been withdrawn or a category of results is restricted.

Dapr pub/sub CEL rules can only access nested JSON values and cannot compare against time (before/after 'now'); designing payloads with JSON-escaped strings or requiring time-based routing forces a work-around that bypasses the DSL.
CloudEvents type strings serve multiple consumers simultaneously for routing, observability and policy enforcement; lax versioning of the type string silently re-routes and re-classifies at once.

A content-derived destination that does not exist is a fatal error, not a fallback: Kafka's TopicNameExtractor fails with a RequestTimeout if the extracted topic does not pre-exist, and auto-creation was rejected because a rogue app could create bogus topics.
KStream branch() arity is fixed at code-compile time while the destination set may be data-driven; the two halves of a dynamic route are not equally dynamic.
An adaptive router with per-instance state behind a load balancer is N different routing policies; Redis-backed cooldown and TPM/RPM tracking is required for correctness, not just performance.

Cross-framework: mixing send-pipeline destination resolution (MassTransit AddMessageRoute, NServiceBus routing stage) with an in-process predicate table (Camel choice, Ballerina match) expresses the routing matrix twice, drifts silently, and cannot be reviewed as one artifact.

Wrong move: routing on XML body fields via broker XPath selectors -> ActiveMQ only evaluates XPath selectors when the Xalan library is on the classpath, so without it the selector fails and the traffic falls through to the default instead of being routed -> instead promote the discriminator to a JMS property and filter with plain SQL-92 header selectors.

Wrong move: deploying the content-based router as in-broker EIP extensions -> routing rules now ride the broker's restart and upgrade cycle and a broken predicate degrades the transport every application shares (ActiveMQ's own documentation weighs this tradeoff explicitly) -> instead keep broker-side filtering to cheap property selectors and run the router as its own application.

Wrong move: growing a static rule table past the point where partners and message types churn -> every onboarding forces an edit plus redeploy of the component all traffic crosses, the exact staleness the Dynamic Router exists to cure -> instead migrate to capability-announcement routing once rules change more often than the topology.
